core: Working definition: medical anthropology is the study of health, illness, and healing across cultures (working definition synthesized from the Society for Medical Anthropology of the AAA and OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology chapter 17)
The disease/illness distinction: disease is the biological condition; illness is the lived, culturally shaped experience
Health systems: every culture has a healing system (ethnomedicine), stated simply with an original example
The honest note that biomedicine is one healing system among many — itself an ethnomedical system rooted in European and North American history and the culture of Western science
Explanatory models: people's own accounts of what is wrong, attributed to Arthur Kleinman
Healing roles: healers across cultures (midwives, herbalists, bonesetters, shamans), with an original example
The honest note: medical anthropology describes health systems; it does not prescribe among them
The honest framing: health is cultural before it is clinical — health and well-being sit at the intersection of biology and culture
supporting: Sickness as the social perception of ill health and the sick role
Medical pluralism: the coexistence of healing systems within one society
Methods: participant observation, illness narrative interviews, cross-cultural comparison without biomedical bias
Applied medical anthropology and cultural competence in health care
Historical roots: Franz Boas and post-World War II public-health engagement
outOfScope: Clinical care and treatment practice (the nursing subject owns it)
Disease mechanisms and pathophysiology (the biology subject owns it)
Mental health as a topic (the psychology subject owns it)
Medical advice, treatment claims, or dosage information — none appear in this lesson
Policy positions on health systems or health-care reform

claims.claim: Medical anthropology is the study of health, illness, and healing across cultures: the Society for Medical Anthropology (a section of the American Anthropological Association) defines it as the subfield that draws on social, cultural, biological, and linguistic anthropology to understand the factors influencing health and well-being, the experience and distribution of illness, the prevention and treatment of sickness, and healing processes; OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology calls it a holistic specialty that draws on all four fields of anthropology, building mainly on cultural and biological anthropology.

Disease and illness are distinct: disease is strictly biological — an abnormality affecting the body's physical structure, chemistry, or function — while illness is the individual's sociocultural experience of a disruption to their physical or mental well-being, shaped by how that illness is viewed, discussed, and explained by the society they live in (OpenStax table of key terms in medical anthropology).

Sickness is the social perception of ill health — the expectations of how a sick person should behave and be treated — and malady is the umbrella term covering disease, illness, and sickness together.

Every culture has a healing system: ethnomedicine is a society's cultural knowledge about the management of health and treatments for illness, and healing specialists — midwives, doulas, herbalists, bonesetters, surgeons, shamans — trained by apprenticeship existed in cultural traditions around the world prior to biomedicine.

Biomedicine is one healing system among many: OpenStax describes biomedicine as an ethnomedical system deeply shaped by European and North American history and rooted in the cultural system of Western science, which draws on biology and biochemistry and validates treatments through clinical trials; medical pluralism occurs when ethnomedical traditions coexist within one society.
Arthur Kleinman's explanatory model holds that asking patients what they think is wrong with them — their own explanations of their illness — can provide valuable information for treatment decisions.

Culture shapes the illness experience and health outcomes: medical anthropologists study this through participant observation, illness narrative interviews, and cross-cultural comparison, and must guard against ethnocentrism — using biomedicine as the unexamined standard for judging other health systems.

Medical anthropology describes rather than prescribes: it compares health systems and analyzes how culture determines how health is perceived, without ranking healing systems, and its applied work recommends cultural competence in health-care training rather than imposing one system on another.

Health is cultural before it is clinical: OpenStax opens chapter 17 by observing that health and a preoccupation with maintaining it permeate all aspects of human culture, that there is no end to the variety of ways cultures across history have treated health, healing, and medicine, and that human health and well-being sit at the intersection of biology and culture.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is biomedicine 'better' than other healing systems?
positions: Biomedicine validates treatments through clinical trials conducted on the principles of the scientific method, which many treat as grounds for its superiority over other systems.

OpenStax notes that biomedicine is itself an ethnomedical system shaped by Western cultural values and history, that it falls short of its ideal of scientific objectivity, and that its presumed superiority rests on the patient's trust in it.
Other ethnomedical systems place their faith in a deity, a healer's power, or time-tested traditional knowledge rather than in the scientific method.
Medical anthropology does not rank healing systems; it compares them descriptively.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents each healing system as cultural, states that biomedicine is one ethnomedical system among many (attributed to OpenStax), and makes no comparative ranking anywhere. No policy or advocacy position is taken.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does taking patients' explanatory models seriously mean rejecting biomedical treatment?
positions: A reader could read Kleinman's model as a claim that patients' beliefs should replace biomedical assessment.

OpenStax's account of the explanatory model recommends that caregivers ask patients what they think is wrong so the answers can inform treatment decisions — it is presented as information-gathering that improves care, not as a rejection of biomedical treatment.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents explanatory models as people's own accounts of illness that carry useful information for care, and it makes no treatment recommendation of any kind — consistent with the field's descriptive stance and this project's no-medical-advice rule.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Machine-generated draft treated as editorial intent only, not evidence; its generic claims (e.g., un-sourced statements that medical anthropology is 'important for understanding health') were replaced with claims that each resolve to a source record.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate lesson with a source-verified lesson (READY_TO_PUBLISH).

Working definition (study of health, illness, and healing across cultures) attributed to the SMA (AAA section) 'What is Medical Anthropology?' statement and OpenStax chapter 17; presented explicitly as a working definition synthesized from those sources.

The disease/illness distinction, sickness, ethnomedicine, biomedicine-as-one-system, Kleinman's explanatory model, healing roles, and the descriptive stance each tied to a source record read on 2026-08-22 (OpenStax chapter 17 sections via Wayback captures of the canonical URLs; SMA and SAPIENS live).
Added the honest note (describes, does not prescribe) and the honest framing (health is cultural before it is clinical) as explicit reality checks, each supported by OpenStax 17.3 / 17-introduction.
All examples are original (Lena and Tomas, Verdan, Ravi, Amara, Ana in Pelago); no source example reproduced.
Added 5 original questions with evidence-backed keys, a verbatim quickCheck (first three items), and 8 source records.
rightsIssues: OpenStax page footer states the book may not be ingested into LLM training or generative AI offerings without permission; therefore all OpenStax records are classified REFERENCE_ONLY with aiIngestionAllowed false, and no OpenStax wording is reproduced — facts are restated in original prose, consistent with the sibling anthropology lessons.

sourceRecords.title: 17 Introduction — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. openstax.org blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture (timestamp 20260317062406) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports the chapter's framing: health permeates all aspects of human culture; medical anthropology is a holistic specialty drawing on all four fields, mainly cultural and biological anthropology; human health and well-being sit at the intersection of biology and culture. Also confirms the chapter outline (17.1 What Is Medical Anthropology, 17.2 Ethnomedicine, 17.3 Theories and Methods, 17.4 Applied Medical Anthropology). Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 17.1 What Is Medical Anthropology? — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. Read via Wayback Machine capture (timestamp 20260711005835) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports the disease/illness/sickness/malady distinction (disease is strictly biological; illness is the individual's sociocultural experience shaped by how society views and explains it; sickness is the social perception of ill health), the WHO health definition context, the Boas history, and the statement that medical anthropology studies how societies construct understandings of health and illness. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 17.2 Ethnomedicine — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. Read via Wayback Machine capture (timestamp 20260416012603) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: ethnomedicine as a society's cultural knowledge about managing health and treating illness; healing specialists (midwives, doulas, herbalists, bonesetters, surgeons, shamans) trained by apprenticeship and existing prior to biomedicine; biomedicine as an ethnomedical system shaped by European and North American history and the cultural system of Western science; medical pluralism as the coexistence of healing traditions. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 17.3 Theories and Methods — Introduction to Anthropology

sourceRecords.title: 17.4 Applied Medical Anthropology — Introduction to Anthropology

sourceRecords.title: 17 Key Terms — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. Read via Wayback Machine capture (timestamp 20260219094048) of the canonical URL on 2026-08-22. Provides glossary definitions used to verify vocabulary: biomedicine (health care systems rooted in European and North American scientific knowledge), ethnomedicine (a culture's traditional knowledge and treatments for the management of health and illness), illness (a person's experience of ill health as defined by their culture), disease (a biological agent that negatively affects health), sickness (the cause of ill health that signifies to others how to treat the person socially), medical pluralism (the use of both ethnomedicine and biomedicine). Reference only; definitions restated in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Can Medical Anthropology Solve the Diabetes Dilemma?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anthropology explainer magazine (live site, read 2026-08-22). Kate Ruder's account of Carolyn Smith-Morris's fieldwork among Pima women with gestational diabetes illustrates how culture, economics, and history shape illness experience and health outcomes, and how anthropologists gather illness narratives in homes and communities. Used to support the claim that culture shapes the illness experience and that anthropologists study it firsthand; no specific statistics from the article are reproduced in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: What is Medical Anthropology?
sourceRecords.provider: Society for Medical Anthropology (section of the American Anthropological Association)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A professional-association statement (live site, read 2026-08-22). The SMA, the AAA's section for the field, defines medical anthropology as the subfield drawing on social, cultural, biological, and linguistic anthropology to understand factors influencing health and well-being, the experience and distribution of illness, the prevention and treatment of sickness, and healing processes. Used as the AAA-side anchor for the working definition; wording restated, not reproduced.
